title: No mark, no caste
hook: the opening stanza says He has no mark or sign, no color, caste or lineage (Jaap 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jaap Sahib, the Tenth Guru's morning praise, and your line, praise at pace. Did you find three quick words for someone? Today, the very first stanza. Day three hundred thirty-three.

A conference badge. Name, company, job title, maybe a little colored dot for vegetarian. Within two seconds of meeting someone, you've read it, and they've read yours. Plenty of life runs on marks like that. Accent, neighborhood, last name, the logo on a shirt: little marks that tell everyone where to put you. In the Tenth Guru's Punjab the marks were sharper still: caste, clan, the sign painted on a forehead, the cut of a robe. And the Tenth Guru opens his great praise by taking every one of those marks and saying: none of these apply. Today: no mark, no caste.
screen: `A BADGE: NAME, COMPANY, TITLE.` → `MARKS THAT TELL US WHERE TO PUT PEOPLE.` → `JAAP OPENS: NONE OF THESE APPLY.`

segments.voice: The first stanza of Jaap Sahib begins with a list of absences. Its opening words, chakr chihan ar baran jaat ar paat nahin jih, mean roughly: the One who has no mark and no sign, no color, no caste, no lineage. Look at that list. Chakr is a mark, the kind of sign some religious groups wore to show which god or sect they followed. Chihan is any sign at all. Baran is varna, the old word for the great classes of Indian society, and it also means color. Jaat is caste. Paat is lineage, the family line. These were the labels that decided, in the Guru's world, who could eat with whom, marry whom, learn which texts, enter which temple. The stanza goes on: form, complexion, outline, dress, nobody can describe them. So before Jaap praises a single quality, it clears the table. Whatever badge you would pin on the Divine, take it off. Here's why that lands for Sikhs. The Gurus had been taking those same badges off people since Guru Nanak. Langar, where everyone sits in one row and eats the same food. Sangat, where anyone may sit before the Guru. And tradition says that when he founded the Khalsa, the Tenth Guru gave its members shared names, Singh and Kaur, so that a surname could no longer announce a caste. Some Sikhs hear the opening of Jaap and the founding of the Khalsa as one idea from two sides: the One has no caste, and so the people who bow to that One shouldn't wear caste either. No mark, no sign.
screen: `NO MARK, NO SIGN, NO COLOR, NO CASTE.` · `THE BADGES THAT SORTED PEOPLE.` · `CLEAR THE TABLE BEFORE THE PRAISE.` · `SINGH AND KAUR: SHARED NAMES.` · then, large: `NO MARK, NO SIGN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drop one label you use for yourself. Pick one: a job title, a school, a type you call yourself, the smart one, the difficult one, the busy one. Hold it in your mind for a breath. Then set it down, as if you were unpinning a badge and laying it on a table. Sit for a little while without it. Who is here when that word is gone? You don't have to answer. Just breathe. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, softly. The bell holds the time.
No mark. The opening of Jaap Sahib: the One has no mark or sign, no color, caste or lineage, and no form anyone can describe.

Your line: no mark, no sign. Today, when you catch yourself sorting someone by a badge, an accent, a job, a neighborhood, take the badge off in your mind and look again. Day three hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs who keep Nitnem recite this opening stanza every morning as the start of Jaap Sahib, and the Gurus' rejection of caste is lived out in langar, where all sit in one row, and in the shared Khalsa names Singh and Kaur.

original.note: Gurmukhi: jaat, caste; one of the labels the first stanza of Jaap says the One does not have.

trapdoor: what you thought: no mark, no caste is just a way of saying God is mysterious.
what it means: the labels that sorted people, sect marks, class, caste, lineage, are all said not to apply to the One.
what a scholar hears: the stanza is a chhappai; its list (chakr, chihan, baran, jaat, paat) names the markers of social and sectarian identity in the Guru's India.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): removed 'most of the world', 'four classes', 'two centuries' and the year 1699 from the voice (not in the cited text; Khalsa naming kept as 'tradition says'), changed 'many Sikhs' to 'some Sikhs'

Opening of Jaap 1 transliterated as 'chakr chihan ar baran jaat ar paat nahin jih' and paraphrased: confirm transliteration and glosses (chakr as a sectarian mark, baran as varna/color, paat as lineage).
The Khalsa names: tradition commonly says Singh for men and Kaur for women were given at or after 1699; the timing of Kaur's general adoption is debated by historians. Phrased as 'tradition says'.
'The Gurus had been taking those badges off people for two centuries': Guru Nanak (b. 1469) to 1699 is about two centuries; confirm wording.
Gurmukhi ਜਾਤਿ for jaat: confirm the form used in Jaap.
